title: The Quran was preserved through two independent channels at once

rows.thesis: The Quran reached us through mass oral memorisation and early written codices at the same time, each checking the other, so a corruption in one would have been caught by the other.
rows.arg:
P1 A text is reliably preserved when it is fixed early and transmitted by many independent people who can check each other. 
 P2 The Quran was memorised in full by many Companions during the Prophet's lifetime, written down under his supervision, gathered into one codex within two years of his death (Abu Bakr, c. 632-634), and copied into a standard edition sent to every major city within about twenty years (Uthman, c. 650). 
 P3 Every later generation recited the whole text publicly (in prayer, especially Ramadan) in front of thousands, and its manuscripts are checked against living memorisers to this day. 
 ∴ The Quran meets the conditions of a reliably preserved text far better than any other scripture of antiquity.
rows.ev:
The written text was not an afterthought. The Prophet ﷺ had scribes such as Zayd ibn Thabit, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Mu'awiya write each revelation as it came, and the Companions recited it in their prayers every day. When many reciters were killed at the Battle of Yamama, Umar urged Abu Bakr to gather the written fragments into one book. Zayd ibn Thabit accepted a passage only if it was found in writing and confirmed by memorisers (Bukhari 4986).

 Under Uthman (c. 650), disputes over regional pronunciations led to an official copy in the Qurayshi dialect. It was made from Abu Bakr's codex (kept with Hafsa) and sent to Kufa, Basra, Damascus and Mecca, and the private copies that differed were burned. The Companions agreed to this, including Ali, who said: "Had I been in his place I would have done the same."

 The modern academic picture backs this up. Angelika Neuwirth, writing in the Cambridge Companion to the Qur'an , notes that newly found fragments support an early fixed text and that the "revisionist" theories of a late, evolving Quran have failed. Seyfeddin Kara ( The Integrity of the Qur'an ) concludes the codex can be dated with certainty to before Umar's death (23/644).

 The radiocarbon-dated Birmingham folios (568-645 CE), the Sana'a lower text and the Hijazi codices such as BnF Arabe 328 show the same surah text in the first Islamic century. Corpus Coranicum lets anyone compare any verse across these early manuscripts. Dated Arabic inscriptions from the same years show the script in use: a tombstone in Egypt is dated Ramadan 29 AH.

إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَحَافِظُونَ
 15:9 
 إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا جَمْعَهُ وَقُرْآنَهُ
 75:17
rows.obj:
"Oral transmission is unreliable."
 For ordinary stories, yes. But the Quran was a fixed text recited word for word, with set rhythm and rhyme, and corrected publicly in congregational prayer. A memoriser who changes a word is corrected by the people behind him. That is the opposite of a game of whispers. And the written channel ran alongside it from the start.


 "Uthman burned copies, so he must have destroyed the real Quran."
 What he destroyed were private copies with dialectal spellings, personal glosses or a different surah order. The text itself was checked against Abu Bakr's codex and against the memorisers still alive, who included the senior reciters. Not one Companion accused Uthman of changing the Quran, even though some of them later fought against him politically. If a verse had been removed, his enemies would have said so.


 "There are variant readings (qira'at), so there are different Qurans."
 See the next argument. The readings were taught by the Prophet himself and are part of the revelation, not later copying errors.

title: Non-Muslim scholars concede the Quran's integrity

rows.thesis: Even scholars hostile or indifferent to Islam admit that the Quran we have is the one Muhammad ﷺ taught.
rows.arg:
P1 A concession from a hostile or neutral witness carries more weight than praise from an insider. 
 P2 A long line of Western orientalists, many of them critical of Islam, state that the Quran is unaltered. 
 ∴ The preservation of the Quran is accepted across the scholarly spectrum; it is not just a Muslim claim.
rows.ev:
William Muir , a missionary-minded critic of the Prophet: "There is probably no other book in the world which has remained twelve centuries with so pure a text."

 Stanley Lane-Poole : there is no doubt of the Quran's authenticity, and it has come down unchanged.

 Kenneth Cragg (Anglican bishop): there is no room for doubt that what we have is essentially what Muhammad taught.

 John Burton : the Quran we have is the text "as it was arranged and approved by the Prophet".

 Andrew Rippin , Neal Robinson , H.A.R. Gibb , R.V.C. Bodley , C.C. Torrey , Denise Masson and Laura Veccia Vaglieri all make similar statements.

 
 Source William Muir on the purity of the Quranic text
rows.obj:
"These are old orientalists; modern scholars are more sceptical."
 The trend is the opposite. The revisionist school of the 1970s (Wansbrough, Crone and Cook) argued for a late Quran, but the manuscript finds since then (Sana'a, Birmingham, Tübingen) have pushed the text back to the Prophet's generation. Neuwirth and Sinai, who are mainstream academics, now treat an early fixed text as the starting point.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Modern scholars like Wansbrough and Crone said the Quran was compiled centuries later.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Their theories predate the manuscript evidence. The Birmingham folios are radiocarbon-dated to 568-645 CE, and Sana'a and Paris codices show the same text in the first century. Even critical scholars like Sinai now say the late-Quran thesis has failed.
rows.sum: From Muir to Neuwirth, scholars who have no stake in defending Islam agree the Quran has not been altered. The manuscript discoveries of the last forty years have only made that consensus stronger.

title: The qira'at are revealed readings, not copying errors

rows.thesis: The canonical readings of the Quran go back to the Prophet ﷺ himself, differ in only a small fraction of words, and complement each other in meaning.
rows.arg:
P1 A copying error is accidental, unsupported by a chain to the source, and usually makes worse sense. 
 P2 Each canonical reading needs a mass-transmitted (mutawatir) chain to the Prophet, must fit the Uthmanic consonantal outline, and must be correct Arabic. The Prophet explicitly approved different readings. 
 ∴ The readings are deliberate, authorised variations within the revealed text, not corruption.
rows.ev:
In Bukhari 2419, Umar heard Hisham ibn Hakim recite Surah al-Furqan differently from how he himself had learned it. He brought Hisham to the Prophet ﷺ, who had both recite and said of each: "It was revealed like this." He added that the Quran was revealed in seven ahruf (modes), "so recite whichever is easy for you".

 Ibn Mujahid's survey found that only about 700 of the Quran's roughly 77,000 words differ between the readings, and almost all of those differences are in vowels or verb forms. They usually add meaning rather than contradict it:

 
 Maliki/Maaliki yawm al-din (1:4): "King of" and "Master of" the Day of Judgement. Both are true of Allah.

 Nunshiruha/nunshizuha (2:259): "We raise them" and "We assemble them". Both describe the bones of the man raised to life.

 
 Ibn Taymiyya compares each reading to a separate verse (Majmu' al-Fatawa 13/391).
rows.ar:
إِنَّ هَذَا الْقُرْآنَ أُنْزِلَ عَلَى سَبْعَةِ أَحْرُفٍ فَاقْرَءُوا مَا تَيَسَّرَ مِنْهُ
 Bukhari 2419
rows.obj:
"If the text was perfectly preserved, why are there differences at all?"
 Because the differences were revealed. Preservation means the text is exactly as it was given, and it was given with these readings. The Bible's variants are the opposite case: they come from scribes changing the text after the fact, as Metzger and Ehrman document (see Corruption of the Bible ).
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Hafs and Warsh are different Qurans, so the Quran wasn't preserved.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer They are two authorised readings, both taught by the Prophet ﷺ (Bukhari 2419), on the same consonantal text, differing in about 1% of words, mostly vowels, with complementary meanings like 'King' and 'Master' of the Day of Judgement. Preservation means preserved as revealed, and it was revealed with these readings.
rows.sum: The readings are authorised by the Prophet, transmitted by mass chains, limited to about 1% of words, and they enrich the meaning. Calling them "errors" misunderstands what they are.

title: The "missing verses" reports answered

rows.thesis: The reports critics cite (the goat, Ubayy's two extra surahs, Ibn Mas'ud's codex, the "valley of gold" and the "200 verses of al-Ahzab") are either weak, or describe abrogation that the Quran itself announces (2:106), or concern supplications rather than surahs.
rows.arg:
P1 A claim of loss needs authentic evidence that a verse the Prophet ﷺ wanted kept in the recited Quran disappeared. 
 P2 Each report either has a weak chain, describes a verse whose recitation the Prophet himself withdrew (naskh al-tilawa), or describes text the Companions themselves did not count as Quran. 
 ∴ None of these reports shows that anything Allah intended for the final Quran was lost.
rows.ev:
The goat that ate the page (Ibn Majah 1944). The "goat" detail comes only through Muhammad ibn Ishaq, a mudallis whose solitary additions are weak (graded weak by al-Arna'ut). The verses mentioned, stoning and the suckling verse, had their recitation abrogated during the Prophet's lifetime while some rulings remained. That is why Imam Malik said the suckling text "is not acted upon". 
 Ibn Hazm: the Companions memorised the Quran, so "a sheep eating a paper changes nothing".

 Al-Baqillani: it is absurd to think the Companions relied on one sheet under a bed.

 


 Ubayy's "two extra surahs" (al-Khal' and al-Hafd). These are the qunut supplication, which Ubayy wrote in his personal codex as a du'a (al-Bayhaqi, al-Sunan al-Kubra 3142). The reports about them have chain gaps of two or three generations. Ubayy himself dictated to Zayd during Uthman's compilation (Kanz al-'Ummal 4789), so he agreed with the final text.

 Ibn Mas'ud's codex "of 111 surahs". No physical codex of his exists. Ibn al-Nadim saw several so-called Ibn Mas'ud codices and none of them agreed with each other. Ibn Mas'ud called al-Fatiha "the seven oft-repeated" and urged reciting the two Mu'awwidhatayn. Three of the canonical readings ('Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i) run through his students, and these include al-Fatiha and the Mu'awwidhatayn. At most, he did not write the short protective surahs in his personal notebook because everyone knew them.

 "If the son of Adam had a valley of gold…" Ibn Abbas said he did not know whether it was from the Quran. Ubayy said they thought it was until Surah al-Takathur was revealed (Bukhari 6440), so it is a hadith or an abrogated wording.

 "Al-Ahzab was as long as al-Baqara." The reports in Musnad Ahmad run through Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad and 'Asim, whose memory was criticised, so they are weak.
rows.ar:
مَا نَنسَخْ مِنْ آيَةٍ أَوْ نُنسِهَا نَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍ مِّنْهَا أَوْ مِثْلِهَا
 2:106
rows.obj:
"Abrogation is just a way of explaining away lost verses."
 Abrogation is announced in the Quran itself: "Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better or similar" (2:106; also 87:6-7). A verse withdrawn by the Prophet ﷺ in his lifetime was not lost; it was removed by the same authority that revealed it. Loss would mean that something meant to stay disappeared, and no authentic report says that.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Aisha said a goat ate the verses of stoning, so parts of the Quran are lost.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The goat detail comes only through Ibn Ishaq, whose solitary additions are weak. The verse's recitation was abrogated in the Prophet's lifetime, as 2:106 allows. And the Companions had memorised the Quran; Ibn Hazm said a sheep eating a page changes nothing.

title: Hadith were written down in the first century, not invented in the third

rows.thesis: Written hadith collections existed in the Companions' and Successors' generation, and their contents match the later canonical books almost word for word.
rows.arg:
P1 If hadith were invented in the 2nd-3rd centuries, first-century collections should either not exist or differ greatly from Bukhari and Muslim. 
 P2 First-century collections such as the Sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih exist, and their texts are almost identical to the same hadith in Ahmad, Bukhari and Muslim. 
 ∴ The canonical collections faithfully preserve earlier material; the hadith were not invented later.
rows.ev:
The Sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih. Hammam was a student of Abu Hurayra (d. 58 AH) and wrote down 138 hadith from him in the mid-first century. The full text survives in manuscript (the Damascus MS) and is quoted whole in Musnad Ahmad. Ninety-eight of its hadith are in Bukhari or Muslim. R. Marston Speight compared the versions ( Der Islam 77, 2000). He found "almost complete identity" and "practically no sign of careless or deceptive practices".

 Tap to enlarge Folios of the Damascus manuscript of the Sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih 
 Source Arabic Literature to the End of the Umayyad Period on the Sahifa of Hammam

 Source Study conclusion: the Sahifa's material is uniformly prophetic hadith, preserved with its chains

 Writing was permitted early. "Do not write from me anything except the Quran" (Muslim 3004) was an early precaution so that the two would not be mixed. The Prophet ﷺ later permitted writing:

 
 "Write for Abu Shah" (Bukhari 2434).

 He told 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr to write, "for only truth comes out of it" (Abu Dawud 3646).

 Ali kept a written sahifa (Muslim 1370).

 Letters were sent out with written rulings, such as 'Amr ibn Hazm's letter and Abu Bakr's book of zakat.

title: The argument from historical precision

rows.thesis: An unlettered man in 7th-century Arabia stated facts about ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia that were unknown in his time, absent from the Bible and Jewish lore, and only confirmed by modern archaeology. The best explanation is a source beyond him.
rows.arg:
P1 If someone with no access to a body of knowledge accurately reports details from it, details unknown to his contemporaries and absent from every source available to him, the best explanation is that he received them from a source with that knowledge. 
 P2 The Quran contains such details: the title "king" for Joseph's ruler but "Pharaoh" for Moses' ruler, Pharaoh's baked-brick tower, the Egyptian motif of heaven and earth weeping for the dead, a deified Pharaoh who still had gods of his own, and Abraham's rejection of the Mesopotamian astral triad. 
 P3 The Prophet ﷺ could not read, never went to Egypt, had no Arabic Bible, and the Bible and midrash either lack these details or get them wrong. Hieroglyphs were unreadable until Champollion (1822) and cuneiform until the mid-1800s. 
 ∴ The best explanation is that the Quran comes from the One who knows the unseen.
rows.ev: Egyptian sources became readable only recently. The Rosetta Stone was found in 1799 and Champollion deciphered it in 1822. Before that, no one in the world, Muslim, Jewish or Christian, could read an Egyptian royal title or funerary text. Cuneiform was cracked by Rawlinson and others in the 1850s. Every detail below was confirmed only after those decipherments.
rows.obj:
"He could have heard these from Jews or Christians in Arabia."
 The test is simple: the details are not in the Jewish or Christian sources. On several of them (Pharaoh's title, the size of the Exodus, the creator-claim of Pharaoh) the Bible actually says the opposite. You cannot copy a correction from the text you are correcting.


 "These are lucky guesses."

title: "King" in Joseph's time, "Pharaoh" in Moses' time

rows.thesis: The Quran calls Joseph's ruler al-malik (the king) and Moses' ruler Fir'awn (Pharaoh). This matches Egyptian history exactly, while the Bible uses "Pharaoh" anachronistically for both.
rows.arg:

 P2 Joseph lived well before that, plausibly under the Hyksos, while Moses lived in the New Kingdom. 
 P3 The Bible uses "Pharaoh" for the rulers of Abraham's and Joseph's eras (Gen 12, Gen 41). The Quran uses "king" for Joseph's ruler (12:43, 50, 54) and "Pharaoh" only for Moses'. 
 ∴ The Quran is precise where the Bible is anachronistic.

 Source British Museum Dictionary of Ancient Egypt (Shaw & Nicholson): before the New Kingdom the use of "pharaoh" is strictly anachronistic

 Source Scholars note the biblical use of "pharaoh" for Joseph's ruler is an anachronism

وَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ إِنِّي أَرَىٰ سَبْعَ بَقَرَاتٍ سِمَانٍ
 12:43

title: Pharaoh's tower of baked brick

rows.thesis: Pharaoh orders Haman to "kindle fire upon clay" to build a tower (28:38). Baked brick was rare in Egypt and appears in the Ramesside period, which is Moses' era.
rows.arg:
P1 Egyptian building was overwhelmingly stone and sun-dried mud brick; fired brick was unusual. 
 P2 Petrie's excavations found fired brick introduced in Ramesside times in the Delta, in a tomb bearing a cartouche of Ramesses II. 
 P3 The Quran describes exactly this technique in Moses' time and pairs it with the royal ambition to "reach the ways of the heavens", which echoes the Pyramid Texts' ladder for the king to ascend to the sky. 
 ∴ The Quran's detail fits the Egyptian evidence for that period.

Tap to enlarge Petrie, Tanis II (1888): "The earliest tomb opened was one built of red baked bricks", in the Ramesside Delta 
 Source The Quran's description: baked clay (kiln-fired brick) and a high structure "to reach the ways of the heavens"

 28:38
rows.obj:
"The Bible's Tower of Babel had baked bricks, so the Quran just moved the story to Egypt."

title: Abraham and the astral triad

rows.thesis: The Quran has Abraham reject a star, then the moon, then the sun (6:75-79). This is precisely the top triad of Mesopotamian religion: Venus (Ishtar), Moon (Sin) and Sun (Shamash).
rows.arg:
P1 In Abraham's Mesopotamia (early 2nd millennium BCE), the leading cosmic gods were Ishtar (Venus), Sin (the moon) and Shamash (the sun), shown together on kudurru boundary stones and seals. 
 P2 The Bible only says Abraham's fathers "served other gods" (Josh 24:2). Jewish legends give different lists: fire, water and earth (Apocalypse of Abraham 7) or "the stars" in the plural (Jubilees 12). 
 P3 The Quran names exactly the triad, in the observational order of an evening sky: Venus as the evening star that sets soon after sunset, then the moon, then the sun. 
 ∴ The Quran reflects the actual religion of Abraham's world, which was rediscovered only by modern Assyriology.

title: More Egyptian details the Bible lacks

rows.thesis: Several smaller details in the Quran's Moses story fit Egyptian evidence better than the biblical account does.
rows.arg:
P1 A cumulative case is built from many independent details that each fit the evidence. 
 P2 The details below each fit Egyptian evidence, and each is either absent from the Bible or contradicted by it. 
 ∴ Together they strengthen the inference that the Quran's source knew Egypt.
rows.ev:
"Neither heaven nor earth wept for them" (44:29). Egyptian funerary texts promise the dead king that "the sky weeps for thee, the earth trembles" (Pyramid Text Utterance 553) and "heaven and earth weep for thee" (Songs of Isis and Nephthys). The Quran inverts the formula for the drowned Pharaoh, a motif only readable after 1822.

 A deified Pharaoh who has gods (79:24 with 7:127). Critics call it a contradiction that Pharaoh says "I am your lord most high" while his chiefs speak of "your gods". New Kingdom kings like Ramesses II were worshipped as divine while themselves worshipping Amun, Ra and Ptah. The Quran describes exactly that.

 The rivers beneath Pharaoh (43:51). In the Quran, Pharaoh boasts of owning the Nile's channels, which is realistic royal propaganda. In Ezekiel 29:3 Pharaoh says "My Nile is my own; I made it ", a creator claim with no Egyptian parallel.

 A small band (26:54). Pharaoh calls the Israelites "a small band". The Bible has 600,000 men, about two million people, leaving Egypt, which archaeology cannot find any trace of. The Quran's number is the plausible one.

 
 Source The Bible has Pharaoh claim to have made the Nile (Ezek 29:3); the Quran has him claim to own the rivers (43:51)

 
 The Samiri (20:85-97). Critics allege an anachronism with "Samaria". But Egyptian shemer means "foreigner/stranger" (Budge, Hieroglyphic Dictionary II p.741), which fits a foreign agitator who led the Israelites to a calf cult reminiscent of the Apis bull.

 
 Source E.A. Wallis Budge, An Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary , vol. II: shemer , "stranger, foreigner"

 
 Pharaoh's body preserved as a sign (10:92). New Kingdom royal mummies survive. The Bible says nothing about Pharaoh's body.

 Haman. Christians say Haman belongs to the Persian court of Esther. But the Quran's Haman is an Egyptian official, and the name is plausibly an Egyptian title (see Silverstein, JSAI 34).

 
 Source The Egyptian background of the name Haman
rows.obj:
"The Quran borrowed Haman from Esther and got the era wrong."
 This assumes there can be only one person with a name or title. The Quran never links its Haman to Persia, to Esther or to Mordecai. And the Egyptian evidence gives a real setting for an official with that title.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “These details are too small to prove anything.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Each is small, but each goes against the Bible and matches Egyptian evidence. A copier doesn't keep correcting his source in the direction of archaeology he can't access.
rows.sum: Weeping heaven and earth, a god-king with gods, rivers he owns rather than made, a small band of Israelites, a foreign "shemer": each detail fits Egypt and departs from the Bible.

title: The Quran's stories are not copied from late legends

rows.thesis: Critics say the stories of Dhul-Qarnayn, the Sleepers of the Cave and Abraham smashing the idols were borrowed from Syriac or rabbinic legends. In each case the supposed source is later than the surah or differs on the points that matter, and where an older tradition exists, the Quran confirms its true core while correcting it.
rows.arg:
P1 Borrowing requires that the source existed before the borrower and that the borrower reproduces its distinctive features. 
 P2 The Syriac Alexander Legend is dated after 628, while Surah al-Kahf is Meccan (before 622); the Quran omits the legend's distinctive (and fabulous) details; and the rabbinic parallels were in Hebrew and Aramaic academies far from Mecca, some compiled after Islam. 
 ∴ The parallels do not show copying. At most they show the Quran confirming true older traditions, as it says it does (5:48).
rows.ev:
Dhul-Qarnayn and the Alexander Legend. The Syriac Alexander Legend is dated by most scholars to around 629-636, celebrating Heraclius' victory, while Surah al-Kahf belongs to the Meccan period. The legend makes Alexander a prophet who calls himself horned by God, has people hiding in caves from the scorching sun, names the kings of Gog and Magog, and describes a gate with iron nails. None of this is in the Quran. The Quran never names him Alexander, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "I do not know whether Dhul-Qarnayn was a prophet or not" (al-Hakim; Sahih al-Jami'). 'Ali explained the name "the two-horned" as referring to blows he received on both sides of his head, not literal horns (Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba). Pre-Islamic Arab poets already knew a Dhul-Qarnayn (Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari ). The Bible itself praises pagan rulers as God's instruments: Cyrus is "My anointed" and "My shepherd" (Isa 44:28-45:1), and Nebuchadnezzar "My servant" (Jer 27:6).

 The Sleepers of the Cave. The story of youths who fled persecution and slept for generations was told by Christians about Ephesus under Decius (c. 250), with Jacob of Serugh (d. 521) writing a homily on it. The Quran tells it with a point the Christian versions lack: people disputed their number, "three, the fourth their dog… five… seven", and "say: my Lord knows best their number" (18:22). The Quran knows the story circulates in variant forms and refuses to settle what is not important.

 Abraham smashing the idols (21:51-70). Genesis Rabbah (38:13, 5th century, Palestine) has a version in which Abraham breaks the idols in his father's shop. The Quran's version is set in his people's temple and focuses on his public argument with them. Islam teaches that true accounts of the prophets can survive in Jewish tradition (the Prophet ﷺ said "narrate from the Children of Israel, there is no harm", Bukhari 3461), and the Quran confirms and corrects. Other alleged sources are later than the Quran: Pirqe de-Rabbi Eliezer , cited for several parallels, refers to Islam and dates to the 8th-9th century, so influence may run the other way, as Michael Pregill and Nicolai Sinai have noted.

 Method. Scholars such as François de Blois and Oliver Leaman warn that in the vast literature of late antiquity, parallels are "almost too easy to find"; similarity is not a model of influence.

title: Answers to "anachronism" charges

rows.thesis: Several details critics call anachronisms (crucifixion in Pharaoh's Egypt, a "dirham" in Joseph's story, monasticism as an innovation, Pharaoh's body preserved) are either accurate or misread.
rows.arg:
P1 A charge of anachronism requires that the word or practice could not have existed in that setting. 
 P2 Each of these has a sound reading in its setting. 
 ∴ These are not errors.
rows.ev:
Crucifixion in Egypt (7:124; 20:71). The Arabic salb covers fastening or suspending a body on a stake or tree, not only the Roman cross. Genesis 40:19 has Pharaoh's baker told that Pharaoh "will hang you on a tree". Scholars of ancient execution (Samuelsson; Chapman) warn against separating crucifixion, impalement and suspension rigidly, and impalement is attested in New Kingdom Egypt.

 "A few dirhams" (12:20). Dirham here means a weight of silver ( Lisan al-'Arab : "a dirham of weight"), and payment in weighed silver is attested in Middle Kingdom Egypt. It is not a minted coin.

 Monasticism "they invented" (57:27). Jesus and the apostles married (Peter, 1 Cor 9:5), and the NT has no command to withdraw into celibate desert life; monasticism began with Antony of Egypt in the late 3rd century. Metzger and Ehrman note that monk-scribes even inserted "and fasting" into several verses (Mark 9:29; 1 Cor 7:5).

 "We will preserve your body as a sign" (10:92). The Quran adds a detail the Bible lacks: Pharaoh's body would be kept as a sign. Royal mummies of the New Kingdom survive today. (The Pharaoh of the Exodus is not identified with certainty, so present this as consistent with the evidence rather than as proof.)
rows.obj:
"Crucifixion was invented by the Persians centuries later."
 The Roman form was, but the Quran's word is general, and the Bible's own Joseph story has an Egyptian king hanging a man on a tree.

title: The splitting of the moon

rows.thesis: The splitting of the moon (54:1-2) is reported by many Companions through independent chains, and the Quraysh's response ("continuous magic") shows they saw something they could not deny. Its absence from other records is expected for a brief night-time event.
rows.caution: Use this defensively. Its strength is the mass transmission and the Quraysh's reaction, not later legends like the Kerala king.
rows.arg:
P1 A public event reported by many eyewitnesses through independent chains, and acknowledged by enemies, is historically credible. 
 P2 The splitting was reported by Ibn Mas'ud, Anas, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Hudhayfa, 'Ali and Jubayr ibn Mut'im, scholars classed it as mass-transmitted, and the Quran records the Quraysh calling it magic, not denying it. 
 ∴ The event is well attested.
rows.ev:
The Quran. "The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split. And if they see a sign, they turn away and say: continuous magic" (54:1-2). The surah was recited publicly in Mecca to the people who would have denied it if nothing had happened.

 The reports. Bukhari and Muslim record it from several Companions; Ibn Kathir and al-Kattani class it as mutawatir . Travellers arriving in Mecca were asked and confirmed seeing it (al-Tayalisi).

 Why not worldwide records? It was night in Arabia and day across much of the world, brief, unannounced, and most people were asleep; record-keeping of the sky was patchy (al-Khattabi, al-Qurtubi). A Kerala tradition that the Chera king Cheraman Perumal saw it and converted exists in Malabar sources, but it is late and should be treated with care.

title: Mecca's antiquity and the People of the Ditch

rows.thesis: Critics say Mecca is unattested before Islam and that the Quran praises Trinitarian martyrs (the People of the Ditch, 85:4-8). Ancient sources point to a revered Arabian sanctuary, and the Najran martyrs' theology is disputed in the Christian sources themselves.
rows.caution: The pre-Islamic evidence for Mecca is suggestive rather than conclusive; Arabia is the least excavated region of the Near East. Present it as consistent evidence, not proof.
rows.ev:
Mecca. 

 
 Diodorus Siculus (1st century BCE, Library of History 3.44) describes a temple in western Arabia "very holy and exceedingly revered by all Arabians"; Edward Gibbon read it as the Kaaba.

 Ptolemy's 2nd-century map lists "Macoraba" in western Arabia, which many scholars (such as Philip Hitti) identify with Mecca.

 The Harran inscriptions of the Babylonian king Nabonidus (6th century BCE) name Yathrib (Medina) and Khaybar among Hijazi towns.

 Anastasius of Sinai (7th century) mentions the Kaaba, and the Quran calls Mecca "Bakka" (3:96), echoing the "valley of Baca" of Psalm 84:6.

 The theory that the first qibla was Petra (Dan Gibson) has been rejected by specialists, who note that the mosque orientations he relies on are imprecise.

 
 The People of the Ditch (85:4-8). The surah praises believers burned in a trench for their faith, usually identified with the Christians of Najran killed by the Jewish king Yusuf (Dhu Nuwas) around 523. Christians argue they were Trinitarians, so the Quran praises Trinitarians. But the Christian sources disagree: the Syriac Book of the Himyarites (a damaged 12th-century manuscript) makes them Miaphysites; Chalcedonian writers claim them as Chalcedonian. Philostorgius records that the Arian missionary Theophilus the Indian converted Himyar around 354, and in the Greek Martyrdom of Arethas the persecutors ask them only to deny "the man called Jesus", not God. Ibn Abbas described them as believers in the oneness of God. The Quran praises them for believing "in Allah, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy" (85:8), and that is what it praises.

title: What makes a prophecy count

rows.thesis: A prophecy is evidence only if it is specific, risky, recorded before the event, and unlikely to come true by chance. The prophecies below meet all four.
rows.arg:

title: The Romans will be victorious (30:2-5)

rows.thesis: The Quran predicted, at the low point of the Byzantine Empire, that Rome would defeat Persia within a few years. It did, against all expectation.
rows.arg:
P1 Around 614-615 CE, Persia had taken Damascus and Jerusalem (carrying off the "True Cross") and soon Egypt. Byzantium seemed about to collapse. 
 P2 At exactly this time, in Mecca, the Quran announced: "The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will overcome, within a few years ( bid' : three to nine)" (30:2-4). 
 P3 Heraclius' counter-offensive began in 622 and destroyed the Persian army at Nineveh in 627, within the stated range. The Quran also said "on that day the believers will rejoice" (30:4), and the Muslims' own victory at Badr (624) fell in the same period. 
 ∴ A specific, unlikely prediction with a time limit was fulfilled.
rows.ev:
Edward Gibbon, no friend of Islam, wrote: "At the time when this prediction is said to have been delivered, no prophecy could be more distant from its accomplishment, since the first twelve years of Heraclius announced the approaching dissolution of the empire."

 Tap to enlarge Tommaso Tesei, "The Romans Will Win!" Q 30:2-7 ( Der Islam 2018) 
 Tesei, a non-Muslim academic, accepts that the verse predicts a Roman victory. His way out is to argue it was edited after the event. That shows how precise the prediction is: the only escape is to deny it was made in time. But the surah is Meccan, the event was famous, and Quraysh would have mocked a failed prophecy. The early sources record a wager on it between Abu Bakr and Ubayy ibn Khalaf (Tirmidhi 3194).

title: The fire of the Hijaz (1256 CE)

rows.thesis: The Prophet ﷺ foretold that a fire would emerge from the land of the Hijaz that would light up the necks of camels in Busra, in Syria (Bukhari 7118, Muslim 2902). It happened in 654 AH / 1256 CE, recorded by eyewitnesses and confirmed by modern volcanology.
rows.arg:
P1 The prophecy is in Bukhari and Muslim, compiled in the 3rd century AH, four centuries before the event, so it cannot have been written after the fact. 
 P2 In 1256 a volcanic eruption at Harrat Rahat near Medina produced lava flows for about 52 days, and its glow was reported as far as Tayma and Busra, roughly 900+ km away. 
 P3 Volcanic eruptions in the Hijaz are rare, and Medina has no other recorded historical eruption. 
 ∴ A specific, unlikely event foretold centuries earlier was fulfilled exactly.
rows.ev:
Contemporary scholars recorded it. 
 Abu Shama al-Maqdisi in Damascus received letters from Medina's judge describing earthquakes and a fire "like a city". People in Tayma wrote letters by its light.

 Al-Qurtubi in Egypt and al-Nawawi in Syria recorded it. Al-Nawawi called the reports mutawatir (mass-transmitted).

 Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Dhahabi confirmed that its light reached Busra.

 


 
 Source Imam al-Nawawi: "A fire broke out during our time in al-Madinah…"

 Source Ibn Taymiyya: the fire broke out in 655 AH and its light was seen in Busra

 
 Modern geology confirms it. The Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program and the USGS record the 1256 Harrat Rahat eruption. A study by El-Masry et al. ("Historical accounts of the AD 1256 eruption near Al-Madinah") reconstructs it from the Arabic eyewitness accounts.

 
 Source Modern geological literature confirms the 1256 Harrat Rahat eruption

 Source Abu Shama al-Maqdisi, al-Dhayl 'ala al-Rawdatayn : an eyewitness-era chronicle of the eruption

 Bukhari 7118
rows.obj:
"Bukhari could have been edited after 1256."
 Bukhari's Sahih was transmitted in many manuscripts and through countless teachers' chains across the Muslim world centuries before 1256. Medieval scholars themselves pointed to this hadith as fulfilled in their own time , which shows it was already well known.

title: The Mongols and the fall of Baghdad

rows.thesis: Authentic hadith describe a people with broad faces, small eyes and flat noses, wearing hair shoes, who would fight the Muslims and descend on a great city by the Tigris. The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, a city that did not exist in the Prophet's lifetime.
rows.arg:
P1 Bukhari 2928 and 3590 describe the Turks/Mongols physically: "small eyes, red faces, flat noses, their faces like hammered shields, wearing shoes of hair". 
 P2 Abu Dawud 4306 (graded hasan) describes a great city "by a river called the Tigris, with a bridge", called "Basra", attacked by Banu Qantura' with broad faces and small eyes, and its people splitting into three groups. 
 P3 The Mongols under Hülegü sacked Baghdad in 1258. Baghdad stood on the Tigris, had bridges and a Basra Gate, and had over a million people. It was founded in 762, more than a century after the Prophet's death. 
 ∴ A detailed description of a people and a city that did not yet exist was fulfilled.
rows.ev:
Ibn Taymiyya, who lived through the Mongol invasions, said that anyone who had seen Genghis Khan's and Hülegü's armies could not have described them more accurately than the Prophet ﷺ did over 600 years earlier (al-Jawab al-Sahih 2/171).

 Source Ibn Taymiyya: anyone who saw these Turks could not describe them better

 The common narrator of Abu Dawud's report, Sa'id ibn Jumhan, died in 136 AH, before Baghdad was built in 145 AH. The report therefore predates the city it describes.
rows.obj:
"'Turks' were known to the Arabs, so describing them is no miracle."
 The point is the whole package: their appearance, their attack on a great city by the Tigris with a bridge, and the three-way split of its people. That city was built after the narrator's death.

title: Barefoot shepherds competing in tall buildings

rows.thesis: Among the signs of the Hour, the Prophet ﷺ said "you will see barefoot, naked, destitute shepherds competing in constructing tall buildings" (Bukhari 50, Muslim 8). Bedouin Arabia, transformed by oil wealth, is now home to the world's tallest buildings.

 P3 Within a century of the oil discoveries, the Gulf states hold the tallest building on earth (the Burj Khalifa) and the Jeddah Tower is under construction to surpass it.  ∴ A specific and improbable social prophecy has been fulfilled.

title: The Trench: keys to Syria, Persia and Yemen

rows.thesis: During the siege of Medina, when the Muslims were outnumbered and starving, the Prophet ﷺ struck a rock in the trench and announced that he had been given the keys of Syria, Persia and Yemen. All three were conquered within about fifteen years.

 P3 For over two thousand years after Abraham, the Arabs had no prophet, no revealed law and no unified monotheism. They gained all three only through Muhammad ﷺ, who was a descendant of Ishmael through Kedar. 
 ∴ The only fulfilment of the promise in the biblical sense is the Prophet ﷺ and his nation.

 Christian writers have conceded it too. The Catholic Abbé de Broglie said the progress of Islam fulfils the promise to Abraham. The Arab Christian apologist Anis Shorrosh, a fierce critic of Islam, admits the Muslim empire fulfilled "I will make him a great nation".

title: Isaiah 29:12: "Read!" "I cannot read"

rows.thesis: Isaiah 29:12 describes a book given to one who is not learned. He is told "Read this", and he replies "I am not learned". This mirrors the first revelation in the cave of Hira, and the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus even reads "Hira".

 P3 In the Septuagint text of Codex Sinaiticus, the original scribe wrote ΧΙΡΑ, which is how Greek renders "Hira". A later corrector changed it to ΧΕΙΡΑΣ ("hands"). 
 ∴ The scene matches the beginning of the Prophet's mission, down to a manuscript that names the cave.

title: The Paraclete (John 14-16)

rows.thesis: Jesus promised "another Paraclete" who would come after him, speak only what he hears, glorify Jesus, convict the world, and guide into all truth. These are the marks of a prophet, not of an abstract spirit, and early Muslims read the Gospel's word as "Ahmad".
rows.arg:
P1 The Paraclete is " another Paraclete" (14:16). Jesus himself was a Paraclete (1 John 2:1), so the next one is another of the same kind, a human messenger. 
 P2 He comes only after Jesus leaves ("if I do not go, he will not come", 16:7). He "will not speak on his own; he will speak what he hears" (16:13, exactly Deut 18:18). He will "glorify me" (16:14), "convict the world of sin" (16:8), and teach "many things you cannot bear now" (16:12). 
 P3 The Holy Spirit was already present before Jesus left: on John the Baptist (Luke 1:15), Elizabeth (Luke 1:41) and the disciples (John 20:22). So the Paraclete's coming cannot be the Holy Spirit's first coming. 
 P4 Muhammad ﷺ came after Jesus, spoke only revelation, honoured Jesus against those who slandered him, convicted the world of sin, and brought a complete law. 
 ∴ The Paraclete fits a prophet after Jesus, and Muhammad ﷺ is the only one who fits.
rows.ev:
The "Holy Spirit" identification is textually unstable. In John 14:26, the Old Syriac Sinaitic palimpsest reads just "the Spirit", without "Holy". C.K. Barrett and George Johnston consider "holy" a possible harmonisation.

 Scholars think the Paraclete was once an independent figure. Raymond E. Brown lists scholars (Spitta, Windisch, Bultmann, Betz) who thought the Paraclete was originally an independent figure, later identified with the Spirit.

 A sceptical NT scholar concedes the point. Robert Price admits the Muslim argument is strong.

 The Greek word may encode "praised". Some argue the Greek encodes "the praised one". Para can mean "in excess" and klētos is related to kleos , "praise/glory" (as in Kleopatra and Periklytos). The Coptic commentator Bakhum Habib notes the reading "Periklytos, the praised".

 
 Source Glenn Nielsen: no English translation captures the Paraclete's roles

 61:6
rows.obj:

Second, the Bible calls prophets "spirits": "do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits… many false prophets have gone out" (1 John 4:1). A true prophet is a "spirit of truth" in that sense, and the Assumption of Moses even calls Moses a "holy spirit".


 "He proceeds from the Father, so he is divine."
 The same verb ( ekporeuomai ) is used for every word that "proceeds from the mouth of God" (Mt 4:4) and for evil that proceeds from the heart (Mt 15:18). It means "sent forth by God's command".


 "Jesus sends him in his name, so Jesus is divine."
 False prophets come "in my name" too (Mt 24:5). "In my name" means as my successor, and Jesus says the Father sends him in answer to Jesus' prayer (14:16).

title: Supporting prophecies: the cumulative case

rows.thesis: Alongside the strongest texts, several more passages point to the same Arabian prophet. Each alone is debatable, but together they form a pattern.
rows.arg:
P1 A cumulative case is stronger than any single text. 
 P2 The passages below each place God's coming revelation in Arabia (Paran, Kedar, Teman, Baca), or describe a figure whose details fit Muhammad ﷺ. 
 ∴ Taken together, they confirm the Quran's claim that he is described in the earlier books.
rows.ev:
Deuteronomy 33:2. "The LORD came from Sinai, rose from Seir, shone forth from Mount Paran, and came with ten thousands of holy ones." That is Sinai (Moses), Seir (Jesus) and Paran (Muhammad). Paran is where Ishmael lived (Gen 21:21), and Eusebius located it south of Aila (Aqaba). The Prophet ﷺ conquered Mecca with 10,000 Companions (Bukhari 4276).

 Source Ibn Ezra on Paran and the Arabian wilderness

 
 Habakkuk 3:3. "God came from Teman, the Holy One from Mount Paran; His praise filled the earth." The nations of Cushan and Midian tremble.

 Isaiah 21:13-17 , the "oracle concerning Arabia": fugitives flee the drawn sword, and "within a year … all the glory of Kedar will fail". The Battle of Badr came within about a year of the Hijra, and the Quraysh (Kedarites) were broken. Isaiah 21:7 has a rider on a donkey and a rider on a camel, which Maimonides read as Jesus and Muhammad.

 Psalm 84:6. Pilgrims pass "through the valley of Baca", making it a place of springs. The Quran calls Mecca "Bakka" (3:96).

 Psalm 72. The desert tribes bow before him, his dominion runs "from sea to sea", "prayer shall be made for him continually; daily he shall be praised". Muslims send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ in every prayer. Solomon, who worshipped idols in old age (1 Kgs 11), hardly fits. Ibn Taymiyya refutes applying it to Jesus.

 
 Source Ibn Taymiyya on why Psalm 72 cannot be Jesus

 
 Daniel 2 and 7. After Babylon, Persia, Greece and a divided Rome comes a kingdom "set up by God" that "breaks all these kingdoms". Islam took Babylon, Persia, the Greek and Roman Levant and Egypt, and finally Constantinople in 1453. John J. Collins notes that later rabbis merged Greece and Rome to make room for Islam as the fourth beast.

 
 Source John J. Collins, leading expert on Daniel, on later rabbinic re-readings of the four kingdoms

 Source The 7th-century Khuzistan Chronicle: the Arabs' victories were by God's aid

 
 Haggai 2:7. "The hemdat (desired one) of all nations shall come." The root ḥ-m-d is the root of Muhammad and Ahmad. In the Song of Songs 5:16, the beloved "chief among ten thousand" is kullo mahmaddim , "altogether desirable".

 Psalm 120-121. The speaker laments that he "dwells among the tents of Kedar" with "those who hate peace: I am for peace, but when I speak they are for war", then is promised that "the LORD will keep your going out and your coming in". Compare Qur'an 17:80: "cause me to enter a truthful entrance and to exit a truthful exit", said of the Hijra and the return to Mecca.

 A pre-Islamic Jewish inscription (Bi'r Hima, 523 CE) of the Jewish Himyarite king Yusuf ends with " mḥmd ", read by some scholars (Taghavi & Heidari, Studia Islamica 2026) as a messianic "Praised One". This fits 2:89: the Jews "used to seek victory through him".

"These are all forced readings."

But the pattern is hard to dismiss: Paran, Kedar, Teman, Baca, ten thousand holy ones, a law for the nations, a praised one. All of it points south, to Arabia, and every one of these texts was in the Jewish Bible centuries before Islam.

title: More passages, and the expectation of an Arabian prophet

rows.thesis: Beyond the main texts, several passages and pre-Islamic Jewish and Christian traditions expected a ruler or prophet from Arabia. They are supporting evidence, best used together.
rows.caution: Each of these is debatable on its own. Present them as a pattern that adds to the stronger texts (Deuteronomy 18, Isaiah 42, the Paraclete), not as standalone proofs.

title: The Quran's literary challenge has never been met

rows.thesis: The Quran challenged the most eloquent Arabs of its day to produce even one surah like it. They had every motive to do so and failed, and that failure is best explained by a source beyond Muhammad ﷺ.
rows.arg:
P1 If a person issues a public challenge that his enemies have every motive and ability to meet, and they fail, the best explanation is that the challenge really could not be met by human beings. 
 P2 The Quran repeatedly challenged its opponents to produce a book like it, then ten surahs, then one surah (17:88, 11:13, 2:23, 10:38). 
 P3 The Quraysh were masters of the Arabic language, were desperate to discredit him, and chose war, boycott and assassination attempts rather than the far cheaper option of producing a surah. 
 P4 Their own leading experts conceded that the Quran was not poetry, soothsaying (kahana) or ordinary speech. 
 ∴ The Quran's inimitability is real, and the best explanation is that it is not the speech of a man.
rows.ev:
The challenge is narrowed step by step. First the whole Quran (17:88: "if mankind and jinn gathered to produce the like of this Quran, they could not produce the like of it, even if they helped one another"), then ten surahs (11:13), then a single surah (2:23, 10:38). The shortest surah, al-Kawthar, is three lines. The bar was set as low as it could go, and it was set in public, in the market culture of Ukaz where poets competed for prizes.

 The opponents' behaviour is the evidence. The Quraysh tried bribery (offering him wealth and kingship), a three-year boycott in the valley of Abu Talib, torture of the weak Muslims, and finally a plot to kill him. A short text in Arabic would have cost them nothing. They did not produce one, and those who later tried, such as Musaylima, produced lines that became a joke in Arabic literature.

 The best witness is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, the most respected literary judge of Quraysh. When the Quraysh asked him what to call the Quran so that pilgrims would avoid it, he rejected each label in turn: it is not poetry, for he knew all its metres; it is not the mumbling of a soothsayer; it is not the speech of a madman. He finally settled on "magic" only because it separates a man from his family, and Surah al-Muddaththir (74:18-25) records exactly this deliberation: "he thought and deliberated… then he said: this is nothing but magic handed down". The verse was recited publicly while al-Walid was alive and he did not deny it.

 Its effect on Arabic itself confirms its status. Arabic grammar (Sibawayh), rhetoric (balagha, al-Jurjani's Dala'il al-I'jaz ) and lexicography were built around the Quran as the highest standard of the language. Western scholarship notes the same: the Legacy of Islam (p. 321) describes the Quran as the standard for Arabic grammar and literary theory.

"Literary quality is subjective. Shakespeare is inimitable too."

The judges were not modern readers but the Arabs who knew the forms best, and they agreed it fitted none of them. Also, Shakespeare never staked his credibility on the claim that no one could match him, and his contemporaries were not trying to destroy him by matching him.

 The attempts that exist (Musaylima, Ibn al-Muqaffa' as alleged, al-Mutanabbi as rumoured) are preserved and recorded by Muslims themselves. A successful imitation would have been the single most useful weapon for the Quraysh, the apostates of the Ridda wars and the later Christian polemicists writing in Arabic, and none of them claims to have produced one.


 "Non-Arabs can't judge, so the argument is useless to them."
 A non-specialist can still judge the historical argument: the experts of the time, who were hostile, conceded it. That is how we accept many expert judgements we cannot check ourselves.

section_title: Miracles, sincerity & the wisdom of the law
title: The Prophet ﷺ refused to exploit the eclipse: an argument from sincerity

rows.thesis: On the day his son Ibrahim died, the sun was eclipsed and people said it was for Ibrahim's death. The Prophet ﷺ publicly denied it, throwing away a "sign" that would have boosted his authority. Impostors do not behave like that.
rows.arg:
P1 A false prophet seeks to strengthen his authority; a true prophet tells the truth even when a falsehood would help him. 
 P2 When the sun was eclipsed on the day his son died, the people attributed it to his grief, a ready-made miracle. The Prophet ﷺ immediately corrected them: "The sun and the moon do not eclipse for the death or life of anyone; they are two signs among the signs of Allah" (Bukhari 1043). 
 ∴ His behaviour fits a sincere prophet and does not fit an impostor.
rows.ev:
The event is historically anchored. Ibrahim, the Prophet's son by Mariya, died in 10 AH, and astronomical tables (NASA's eclipse catalogue) record an annular solar eclipse visible over Medina on 27 January 632 CE, matching the date in the reports. So this is not a pious legend built after the fact; it is a datable event.

 The point is psychological and historical. At this moment the Prophet ﷺ was grieving and the people were offering him, unprompted, a cosmic endorsement. A man inventing a religion for power would have stayed silent or accepted it. He instead gathered the people, led the eclipse prayer, and gave a sermon to correct the superstition.

 This fits a wider pattern that even non-Muslim historians have noted. W. Montgomery Watt argued that his readiness to suffer persecution, the high character of those who followed him, and the greatness of what he achieved all make sincerity the default explanation, and that treating him as an impostor raises more problems than it solves. section_title: Miracles, sincerity & the wisdom of the law
title: Prohibitions vindicated: alcohol

rows.thesis: The Quran's total ban on intoxicants (5:90-91) anticipated what modern public health now concludes: there is no safe level of alcohol, and its social costs are enormous.
rows.arg:
P1 A law code reflects divine wisdom if it identifies a harm correctly and legislates the effective remedy, especially if the remedy was not obvious at the time. 
 P2 7th-century Arabia drank heavily and wine was central to its poetry; the Quran nevertheless banned it gradually and then completely, and named its harms: enmity, hatred, and turning people from remembrance and prayer (5:91). 
 P3 Modern medicine and criminology confirm that alcohol has no safe level and drives violence, accidents and family breakdown. 
 ∴ The ban is a mark of wisdom beyond the culture it addressed.
rows.ev:
The ban came in stages, each adapted to a society that loved wine: first noting that its harm outweighs its benefit (2:219), then forbidding prayer while intoxicated (4:43), then the final prohibition (5:90-91). The Companions poured their wine into the streets of Medina when the final verse came (Bukhari 2464).

 The modern data:

 
 In 2023 the WHO stated that "no level of alcohol consumption is safe" for health, since alcohol is a group 1 carcinogen.

 In the US, about 30% of traffic deaths involve an alcohol-impaired driver (CDC: 11,654 deaths in 2020).

 Alcohol is involved in roughly 40% of violent crime and in a majority of domestic-violence incidents in many studies.

 Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders may affect up to 1 in 20 US schoolchildren (May et al., JAMA 2018).

 Studies consistently find religiosity protects against substance abuse.

 
 Note the Quran's diagnosis: it names social harm (enmity and hatred) before spiritual harm. That is exactly what the crime and domestic-violence numbers show.

section_title: Miracles, sincerity & the wisdom of the law
title: Zakat and the economics of mercy

rows.thesis: Islam built a compulsory, rule-based welfare system into worship itself, and history records periods where it virtually eliminated poverty.
rows.arg:
P1 A religion's law shows divine wisdom if it secures justice for the weak in a durable, practical way. 
 P2 Zakat is a fixed annual levy (2.5% on hoarded wealth above a threshold, other rates on crops and livestock) that must go to eight named categories, starting with the poor and needy (9:60). Islam also bans interest (riba), which transfers wealth from borrowers to lenders. 
 P3 Under rulers who applied it, such as Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (r. 717-720), sources report that collectors could find no poor people to receive zakat. 
 ∴ Zakat is a practical, proven system of social justice, which is what we would expect from a divine law.
rows.ev:
Unlike voluntary charity, zakat is a pillar of Islam, as obligatory as prayer. Abu Bakr fought those who refused to pay it after the Prophet's death, which shows it was treated as a right of the poor over the rich, not a favour. The public treasury (Bayt al-Mal) also supported non-Muslims in need: Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported to have granted a stipend to an old Jewish man he found begging.

 T.W. Arnold's The Preaching of Islam (pp. 54, 117) records that dhimmi communities prospered under Muslim rule. The Quran also promises that charity increases rather than reduces wealth (2:261, 2:276), which fits behavioural research showing that giving increases well-being.
rows.ar:

 9:60 
 يَمْحَقُ اللَّهُ الرِّبَا وَيُرْبِي الصَّدَقَاتِ

rows.obj:
"Modern welfare states do this better."

section_title: Miracles, sincerity & the wisdom of the law
title: The 360 joints and the medical hadith: use with care

rows.thesis: Some hadith make claims about the body or medicine that are sometimes presented as scientific miracles. They are best used defensively, to show they are not absurd, rather than as primary proofs.
rows.caution: These arguments depend on how terms are defined and on small or preliminary studies. Don't lead with them. Use them when an opponent claims a hadith is ridiculous.
rows.arg:
P1 A critic who calls a hadith "obviously false" must show it contradicts established knowledge. 
 P2 The hadith of 360 joints, the fly hadith and the camel milk hadith each have plausible readings that are consistent with, or partly supported by, modern findings. 
 ∴ These hadith cannot be used as proof that the Prophet ﷺ spoke falsely.
rows.ev:
360 joints (Muslim 1007). "Every human being is created with 360 joints", given as the reason each person owes a daily charity for every joint. Counts depend on what is called a joint; anatomy references give figures around 360 for synovial and other articulations, while broader counts that include all fibrous junctions reach higher (Vizniak gives about 472). The point is that 360 is a respectable count, not a guess that anatomy contradicts. Chinese and other ancient sources that mention 360 or 365 do so for calendar or cosmological reasons, and were not accessible to the Prophet ﷺ.

 The fly hadith (Bukhari 3320). "If a fly falls into your drink, dip it fully, then remove it, for in one wing is a disease and in the other a cure." Classical scholars like al-Shashi read it as practical advice (irshad), not a command. Laboratory studies have reported antimicrobial activity in house-fly extracts and peptides (for example a 2023 review of Musca domestica antimicrobial peptides, PubMed 36619234), and some small studies report that dipping reduced bacterial counts. This is enough to show the hadith is not absurd; it is not enough to build a "miracle" on.

 Camel milk and urine (Bukhari 233). The Prophet ﷺ prescribed these to a group of desert Arabs with a specific illness. Camel milk has documented bioactive properties. On urine, be cautious: modern health authorities warn against it because of MERS, and the hadith is about a specific remedy for specific people, not a general instruction. Yasir Qadhi and others classify much "prophetic medicine" as the Prophet's ﷺ human experience of his environment rather than revelation, citing the date-pollination hadith ("you know best the affairs of your world", Muslim 2363).

 Ramadan fasting. Studies report benefits such as improved gut microbiome diversity, lower blood pressure, and reduced oxidative stress during Ramadan. These are good illustrations of wisdom in the law, but they are not proofs of revelation.
rows.obj:
"Then why mention them at all?"
 Because critics use them as ridicule ("Islam says dip flies in your drink"). Your goal is to neutralise the ridicule, not to win a proof.


 "The Prophet's medical advice could be wrong under your own view."
 Yes. Muslim scholarship distinguishes his role as a messenger from his ordinary human knowledge of agriculture or local medicine (Muslim 2363). Whether a given medical hadith is revelation is itself a scholarly question.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Your prophet told people to drink camel urine. How can anyone take that seriously?”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer It was a specific remedy for a specific group in a desert setting, following practice known to the Arabs; it is not a general command. Many scholars regard such medical advice as the Prophet's experience as a man of his environment, as he said in Muslim 2363. It tells us nothing against his prophethood, any more than the Bible's medical laws do.
rows.sum: The 360-joint, fly and camel-milk hadith are defensible but not decisive. Use them to show critics have no real case, and build your positive case on stronger ground.

title: "The fastest-growing religion" is not a proof

rows.thesis: Islam's growth is real, but most of it is demographic, so use it as context, never as an argument for truth.
rows.caution: This is not an argument for truth. Use it only to correct someone who says Islam is dying or that its people are leaving en masse.
rows.ev: Pew Research Center's report on 2010-2020 found Muslims were the fastest-growing major religious group, adding about 347 million people. Most of that growth comes from a young age profile and higher fertility, with switching playing a small role. Christianity, by contrast, lost more through switching than any other group.
rows.obj:
"Popularity doesn't make something true."
 Agreed, and you should say so first. Growth is a fact about people, not a proof about God.

Your opponent says
 “Islam only grows because Muslims have more children.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Correct, and I would never use growth as a proof. The arguments for Islam are the Quran's preservation, its challenge, its prophecies and the evidence for God; growth is not one of them.

title: The Quran restores the honour of the prophets

rows.thesis: The Bible attributes idolatry, murder and indecency to the prophets; the Quran retells the same stories and clears them. That is consistent with one source correcting another.
rows.arg:
P1 Prophets are God's chosen examples (6:90); a book that makes them idolaters or murderers undermines the purpose of sending them. 
 P2 The Bible says Aaron made the golden calf, Solomon worshipped idols, Moses committed premeditated murder, and Isaiah walked naked for three years. 
 P3 The Quran retells each story and removes the sin or explains it. 
 ∴ The Quran's versions preserve the logic of prophethood; the biblical versions break it.

Aaron and the calf. Exodus 32:2-5 says Aaron collected the gold, fashioned the calf and built an altar for it. The Quran attributes the calf to "al-Samiri" and has Aaron warn the people: "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my order" (20:90). Moses then interrogates Samiri, not Aaron (20:95-97). Aaron was the high priest God appointed; it makes no sense that he would build the idol and keep his office.

 Moses and the Egyptian. Exodus 2:12: Moses "looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand", a premeditated killing. The Quran: Moses struck the man in a fight to defend an Israelite and he died; Moses immediately said, "This is from the work of Satan… My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me", and he was forgiven (28:15-16). A manslaughter followed by repentance, not a murder followed by concealment.

title: The Quran corrects historical and narrative details

rows.thesis: In several stories the Quran quietly differs from the Bible on a factual detail, and in each case the Quran's version is the more plausible one.
rows.arg:
P1 If the Quran merely copied, its details would match its source, including the source's errors. 
 P2 In the Exodus numbers, the Garden story and Zechariah's sign, the Quran deliberately differs, and the difference resolves a problem in the biblical account. 
 ∴ The Quran is correcting, not copying.
rows.ev:
The size of the Exodus. Exodus 12:37 says 600,000 men on foot left Egypt, besides women and children, implying two to three million people. No archaeology supports a population that size in Sinai, and it would have outnumbered Egypt's army. The Quran has Pharaoh call them "a small band" (26:54).

 The serpent told the truth in Genesis. In Genesis 2:17 God warns that "on the day you eat of it you will surely die"; the serpent says "you will not surely die… your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil" (3:4-5). Adam and Eve do not die that day, and God then says "the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil" (3:22). Read literally, the serpent was right and God was wrong. In the Quran, Satan is the liar: he calls it "the tree of immortality and a kingdom that will not decay" (20:120), which is false.

 Moses' hand. Exodus 4:6 says Moses' hand became "leprous, like snow". The Quran says it came out "white, without any harm" (20:22, 27:12, 28:32), a sign of honour rather than disease.

 Zechariah's silence. Luke 1:20 says Zechariah was struck mute as a punishment for doubting the angel. In the Quran, Zechariah asks for a sign, and silence for three days is the sign granted (3:41, 19:10). Classical commentators such as al-Samarqandi call it a miracle, not a punishment.

 The Israelites' words at Sinai. In Deuteronomy 5:27 the Israelites promise "we will hear and we will do" (Hebrew shama'nu ve-'asinu ). The Quran reports: "they said, we hear and we disobey" ( sami'na wa 'asayna , 2:93; 4:46). The Arabic is a pointed play on the Hebrew: 'asinu (we will do) becomes 'asayna (we disobeyed), summarising their record after the covenant. This is a detail no one in Mecca could have constructed without knowing the Hebrew phrasing.
rows.ar:
إِنَّ هَٰؤُلَاءِ لَشِرْذِمَةٌ قَلِيلُونَ

 فَوَسْوَسَ إِلَيْهِ الشَّيْطَانُ قَالَ يَا آدَمُ هَلْ أَدُلُّكَ عَلَىٰ شَجَرَةِ الْخُلْدِ وَمُلْكٍ لَّا يَبْلَىٰ
 20:120 
 قَالُوا سَمِعْنَا وَعَصَيْنَا

"Pharaoh calling them a small band is just his propaganda."

title: The Quran shows knowledge of the scriptures, and cites them accurately

rows.thesis: Where the Quran explicitly cites earlier scripture, the citation is accurate, and its themes match the earliest layers of the Jesus tradition rather than later Christian theology.
rows.arg:
P1 If the Quran cites a passage of the Psalms correctly and its portrait of Jesus matches the earliest reconstructed sayings source, its author had accurate knowledge of earlier revelation. 
 P2 Quran 21:105 cites Psalm 37:29 almost word for word, and the Quran's Jesus resembles the Jesus of the "Q" sayings source and the Epistle of James. 
 ∴ The Quran's relationship with earlier scripture is that of a revelation recovering what was original, as it claims (5:48).
rows.ev:
Psalm 37:29 in Quran 21:105. "We have written in the Psalms (al-Zabur) after the Reminder: My righteous servants shall inherit the land." Psalm 37:29: "The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell in it forever." This is the only place where the Quran explicitly quotes a named book, and the quote is exact in meaning.

 "Lord of the worlds". The Quran's opening praise, rabb al-'alamin , matches the Jewish liturgical title ribbon kol ha-'olamim ("Master of all worlds").

 The "Q" source. The hypothetical sayings source shared by Matthew and Luke presents Jesus as a teacher of charity, prayer and repentance who works healings, condemns the killing of the prophets (Luke 11:47-51; compare Quran 2:61, 3:21), and is accused of sorcery (Luke 11:15; compare Quran 5:110, 61:6). It has no birth narrative of a divine Son and no atonement theology. This is the Jesus of the Quran.

 The Epistle of James , from the Jerusalem church that stayed loyal to the Law, also reads like the Quran: say "if the Lord wills" before planning (James 4:13-15; Quran 18:23-24); trials refine faith (James 1:2-4; Quran 2:155); do not favour the rich (James 2:1-9; Quran 80:1-10); faith without works is dead (James 2:17-24; the Quran's constant "those who believe and do righteous deeds").

 The Shahada pattern. title: The Torah's own history records loss, rewriting and scribal falsification

rows.thesis: The Hebrew Bible itself says the book of the law was lost for generations, that scribes falsified it, and that many inspired books are gone, which is exactly what the Quran describes (2:79).
rows.arg:
P1 A book that records its own loss and its own scribes' corruption cannot claim perfect preservation. 
 P2 The Hebrew Bible records that the "book of the law" was found in the Temple under King Josiah after it had been forgotten, that the prophet Jeremiah accused the scribes of a "lying pen", and it cites about twenty books that no longer exist. 
 ∴ By its own testimony, the Torah was not preserved in the way the Quran was, which confirms the Quran's account of the earlier scriptures.
rows.ev:
The book that was found. In 2 Kings 22:8 (2 Chr 34:14), the priest Hilkiah "found the book of the law" in the Temple during repairs, and King Josiah tore his clothes on hearing it because his people had not obeyed it. 2 Kings 23:22 adds that "no such Passover had been kept since the days of the judges". In other words, the central law had been lost or ignored for centuries.

 The lying pen of the scribes. Jeremiah 8:8: "How can you say, 'We are wise, and the law of the LORD is with us'? But behold, the lying pen of the scribes has made it into a lie." The Quran: "Woe to those who write the book with their own hands, then say 'this is from Allah' to buy with it a small price" (2:79). Jeremiah 8:10 even adds the motive: "everyone is greedy for unjust gain".

 Contradictions about sacrifice. Jeremiah 7:22: "I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices on the day I brought them out of Egypt"; Amos 5:25 asks, "Did you bring me sacrifices… forty years in the wilderness?" Yet Leviticus is full of sacrificial laws given in the wilderness. The prophets appear not to know the Levitical code as Mosaic.

 Lost inspired books. The Bible cites the Book of the Wars of the LORD (Num 21:14), the Book of Jashar (Josh 10:13; 2 Sam 1:18), the chronicles of Nathan, Gad, Shemaiah and Iddo, and Solomon's 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs (1 Kgs 4:32): about two dozen works in all.

 Ezra and the restoration. Nehemiah 8 shows Ezra reading and re-establishing the law after the Exile; the Jewish apocalypse 4 Ezra 14 even says the books were burned and Ezra rewrote them by inspiration.

 Modern scholarship. The documentary hypothesis holds that the Torah combines several sources (J, E, D, P), visible for example in the two different orders of creation in Genesis 1 and 2 (Richard Friedman, Who Wrote the Bible? ). Many scholars date Deuteronomy to Josiah's time, partly because its curses (Deut 28) follow the pattern of Esarhaddon's 7th-century vassal treaties.

rows.obj:
"Jeremiah 8:8 means the scribes misinterpreted the law, not that they changed the text."
 The verse says the pen (Hebrew 'et , a stylus) of the scribes made it a lie, which points to writing. Ellicott's commentary takes it to refer to written work. Either way, a prophet accused the custodians of the law of falsifying it, which is the Quran's charge.


 "Lost books were never meant to be scripture."
 David ordered the Book of Jashar to be taught (2 Sam 1:18), and Solomon's proverbs and songs were wisdom from God by the Bible's own account. Their loss shows God did not preserve every inspired text of Israel, so "God would never let His word be lost" is not a biblical principle.


 "The documentary hypothesis is disputed."
 The details are, but that the Torah is composite and was edited over centuries is the mainstream view, and you do not need any particular version to make the point.

Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Scrolls reads "sons of God" where the Masoretic text has "sons of Israel", a theological change.
